subtopic: NATIONAL ROUND TABLE ON THE ENVIRONMENT AND THE ECONOMY ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure once again to have an opportunity to debate Bill C-72, an act to establish the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy.
I simply want to say we have waited some time for this opportunity and I am pleased it is happening today. I think this is an excellent initiative. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the round table has essentially been constituted and this will really give it the formal acknowledgement and recognition it so justly deserves.
I know there are others who wish to share their comments on this so I will keep my comments extremely brief.
We have some concerns in terms of this particular bill. It may give the impression that the government is very serious in terms of dealing with some significant environmental issues confronting the country. I think it may be that, but we hope it is much more. We hope it can set the stage for a much greater set of initiatives in the future. When we look around Canada today and consider the commitment, or lack of commitment to environmental assessments on some of the critical major resource projects in the country, we wonder just how serious the government is.
At this point I want to say we support Bill C-72 with some enthusiasm. I look forward to the discussions that will occur later once this gets to committee.

subtopic: NATIONAL ROUND TABLE ON THE ENVIRONMENT AND THE ECONOMY ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I will not be quite so brief. We have a number of things to say concerning the bill. However we reiterate our general support for the bill and in particular our support for the work of the round table.
At the same time we must express some concerns, which we will be raising in committee, about the independence of the round table now that it is to be established in legislation. We have seen a number of situations where other independent bodies that were set up to provide independent advice to Canadians, government and Parliament were jeopardized in their independence. In some cases they were in fact eliminated when the government was not entirely happy to have the advice it was getting from such bodies as the Economic Council of Canada, the Science Council of Canada and numerous others that we have debated in this House at length.
As I said, I do want to pay tribute to the round table for some of the excellent work that has been done. It has played a co-ordinating role with respect to the provincial round tables to ensure the bringing together across Canada of environmental, business and labour organizations and numerous interests in Canadian society, to address this all-encompassing and urgent issue of sustainable development. This work of the round table has been extremely valuable and has laid a good foundation for its future work.
It has produced some excellent reports and is in the process of producing more. The report that was done on the road to Brazil concerning the earth summit and Canada's role with respect to the earth summit was significant in the contribution that private organizations, government and parliamentarians were able to make at the earth summit.
I note as well its significant work on greening agriculture and keeping an eye on trade developments as they affect the environment and our objectives of sustainable development. There has been ongoing work on trade, the environment and competitiveness and I think one of their more recent reports was on the tax aspects of ecologically sensitive lands.
Globally, it is looking at opportunities for government action to require and impose protection of the environment. At the same time it is looking at those things in the system that can actually punish people who do what we really want them to do.
The role of the round table is fundamental to changes we need to make in how we function as a society and a government. We must ensure we have the resources for a sustainable future so we can enjoy prosperity and
March 11, 1993

preserve the very fragile ecosystem upon which we depend for life.
To do that, it is not enough for governments to act. It requires the full participation of all citizens of all interests in Canadian society. In a sense, that is the process the round table has begun and will continue. We see a great need to bring together the many different forces at work to try to implement what we have recently started to understand, that how we operate as human beings in this world, especially when it comes to economic activity, is devastating our very ability to survive on this earth.
We have a number of different actors in the field and there is going to be a very important need in the next short while to ensure that all those forces are working together toward the same objective.
We came away from Rio knowing that transparency, doing things openly, publicly and with the participation of all sectors of our communities is essential to solving some very fundamental problems. I believe one of the challenges facing the round table is how to bring the public into the dialogue. How do we ensure that the very valuable work it has done and continues to do gets the kind of public dissemination that leads to real action at all levels?
At the same time we must ensure that the process is participatory. The public should be involved in the dialogue as issues are addressed. It should not merely be presented with recommendations as to what needs to be done and then expected to come on board. What is needed above all is political will on all sides of this House, at all levels of government and in all areas of human activity. There is no pure environmental issue anymore. On the other side of that statement, there is no issue that is not environmental.
I want to review a few of the issues that have become urgent with respect to the environment and to perhaps demonstrate how far short we are of where we need to be. I want to deal with some specific areas of public policy that I feel have been inadequately addressed.
Public policy must be consistent with the mandate being given to the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy and the tremendous job it and all other organizations in Canada have ahead of them to
Government Orders
start truly protecting this world for our children and our grandchildren.
Let me talk about the green plan. This is a good example where words are not enough. The green plan was tabled with great fanfare and great expectation in 1990. Since then we have seen a pretty steady whittling away of the commitment to the green plan. We saw almost immediately a budget that was supposed to be $3 billion over five years transformed into a $3 billion budget over six years. That translated into better than a 20 per cent cut in the very first year of the green plan. There were cuts in last year's budget and we saw further reductions. The same thing happened again this year.
What initially was supposed to be an expenditure of over $550 million in this year on the green plan was reduced to $415 million and then further reduced to less than $400 million. In each of the years since the green plan was tabled the resources to actually implement it have been steadily reduced.
The other fundamental thing that we have come to understand about protecting our environment is that it is a very complex issue that goes to the very heart of how we relate to other peoples of the globe.
We know now that environmental degradation will come from growing population, growing demands for prosperity around the world, growing demands for energy. We know that poverty is the greatest destroyer of the environment as people destroy their soil, destroy their forests simply in an attempt to survive.
What that means for countries like Canada with all the resources and with all the wealth we have, is that if we are sincere about saving this globe for future generations then we need to be sincere about saving the people of today from poverty, starvation, rampant disease, unclean water, not just in our own country but around the world.
That is why it is tragic the direction that is now being taken with funding for development aid and withdrawing hundreds of millions of dollars from what we provide to help the poorest of the poor in the world. This has been Canada's policy on development aid for well over a decade now. To start taking money away is undermining all that we are asking the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy to do. To take money from those who are hungry and give to those who can

March 11, 1993
Government Orders
spend where it will most benefit our trade is nothing short of immoral.
We know that just small amounts of money, well spent on basic health care, on the education of women, will do more to save our environment than building megaprojects, whether it is dams or huge energy facilities. Yet we seem to have trouble learning that very basic lesson, that a small amount of money spent on human development is the most important thing we can do for our world. So we see a shift of money away from those in the world who most need it to where it is going to help us trade better and make more profits.
At home we have not even addressed how we are going to cut our own energy use. We keep taking money out of energy conservation and alternative energy sources and putting it into megaprojects for energy production, encouraging us to be more consumptive and more wasteful. This is exactly the opposite direction to what would be indicated by the kind of work, the kind of onerous responsibility we are asking the national round table to take on and which it has been taking on.
We have not addressed the issues of how our trade affects poverty around the world and the pressures on the environment resulting from that poverty. It is shameful that in 1993 the richest countries of this world take from the poorest $50 billion a year more than we put into them and now we who consider ourselves one of the most progressive nations of the world have just said we are going to put even less into those poorest countries. We are profiting from their poverty and our earth, our air, and our water are the victims of that profit.
We have seen government refusing to take its responsibility and play a leadership role by even looking at its own operations and ensuring we are conducting the business of government in the most environmentally sound way possible. We have ignored our own legislation on environmental assessment to the destruction of the environment and of our own aboriginal people.
We are continuing a world where 20 per cent of the population consumes 80 per cent of its wealth and resources. If we are serious about the job we are now formally and legally giving the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy, we have to look first to ourselves in this Chamber, to those who are in the
cabinet room, to heed the lessons and the wisdom that have already come from the round table and to act in ways that are supportive of their mandate, not destructive.
The round table has played a crucial role in bringing many different forces together in creating a focus and a force for change that must keep growing if we are to leave the next generation a world that is even habitable, much less prosperous.
We look forward to supporting this bill, seeing it go to committee and discussing the legislation in particular in committee.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to rise today in support of an action that is in the interest of all Canadians, and that is Bill C-72, an act to establish the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy.
Canada has a very distinguished history in environmental leadership dating back to early in this century. We are a protector of great natural resources. It has been of interest to Canadians and the establishment of the Commission of Conservation in 1909 was in retrospect a far-sighted action for any government then existing.
In 1972 Canadians supported and played a leadership role in the ground-breaking Stockholm Conference on Human Environment. Then in the 1980s, Canadians led the way in building international consensus and preparing the original world conservation strategy and its recent successor Caring for the Earth.
A few years ago in this Chamber, I think it was in 1987, we had an opportunity to debate at some length the World Commission on Environment and Development. This was a United Nation's report, commonly called the Brundtland commission or Our Common Future. The commission was put forward by the United Nations, chaired by the then Prime Minister of Norway, Madam Gro Brundtland. We had two Canadian representatives. A very distinguished Canadian, Jim McNeill, was the secretary of the Brundtland commission. In the report it had a recommendation that there would be round tables where people from different parts of the community could come together and discuss issues that were important to the environment.

Canada's National Task Force on the Environment and Economy prepared the earliest and still the most comprehensive national response to the challenges that were presented by the Brundtland commission. It was not all talk. There have been a lot of reports about the environment, but this was a very significant report. In response to the task force each province and territory in Canada and the federal government established round tables to address the pressing issues of sustainable development. This round table involved people from all sectors of our community coming together, sitting down at a table and building a consensus.
There are now dozens of local round tables across the country. Some municipalities have now established round tables. In my own constituency of Scarborough Centre, we have just recently started the process of getting this round table set up by bringing people together. These round tables are established all across the country in municipal and regional areas to discuss the conflict for the common good of bringing people together. These uniquely Canadian round tables have two things in common.
First, unlike previous associations and interest groups, their members have divergent interests and opinions, but a common interest in resolving problems of environment and economy. Second, they have a remarkable record of achievement, based on open discussion and consensus decision-making. While in 1987 it seemed terribly naive to suggest that Canada would launch dozens of new institutional experiments in democracy in response to a United Nations' report, a task force of industrial leaders, the environment minister, and environmentalists from all parties recommended exactly that and that is exactly what happened. Canadians right across the countiy in every province and the two territories formed an entirely new institution to address the new challenges of this new concept called sustainable development.
This past summer Canada was a very energetic and enthusiastic participant at the unprecedented earth summit held in Rio de Janeiro in June of last year. The delegation from Canada was extensive, made up of members from all the parties in the House of Commons, as well as numerous environmental groups and non-government groups. Many people gathered in Rio de Janeiro to discuss these issues some 20 years after the
Government Orders
Stockholm conference. It was truly the largest United Nations conference of any proportions and uniquely it was concerning the environment.
The Minister of the Environment led the delegation for that two-week conference in Brazil. Our Prime Minister was there to give an address on behalf of Canada and to sign two very important conventions, the biodiversity convention and the global warming convention. More important, we were leading the way. As other countries were concerned about signing the biodiversity convention, our own Prime Minister said: "We will be the first to sign this convention". Indeed, the Prime Minister did sign on behalf of Canada, the first nation to sign that biodiversity convention to protect the flora and fauna of the earth.
In this regard the process of setting up a round table was a most important aspect of what we were wanting to do in terms of having organizations and people from all different walks of life come together and have this round table as a meeting of the minds.
I might say in response to my colleague who just spoke concerning Canada's green plan, the United Nations Environment Program chairman, Mr. Tolba, stated at the Brazil conference that Canada's green plan was an example for all nations. It was hailed as the example of what Canadians could do together and as a nation come forth with a green plan. In fact nations that participated in that conference were anxious to find out what the green plan was. They wanted us to tell them about the plan, to give them copies of it.
The $3 billion in funds attached to the commitments of the green plan is a very, very substantial commitment on behalf of all Canadians. This year alone there is a 30 per cent increase in the amount of funds attached to the environment programs, initiatives that take place out of that green plan. As we are pressed in terms of our financial resources, our commitment to the environment has been steadfast in the increase of that amount of money.
At a time in history when all of us need some encouragement about our ability to respond to rapid change, we have an opportunity to build on our tradition of forward-looking institutional adaptation in the interests of improving our environmental and economic quality of life.

The United Nations recently named Canada as the best place in the world in which to live. We are very proud ol that and I believe that Canadians are proud. We want to keep it that way, with our social structure, with our opportunities for people to fulfil their lives, our health care, our educational system. All of those items are very important in terms of our quality of life and the United Nations has recognized that.
The purpose of Bill C-72 is to bring people together to help ensure that Canadians working together will keep it the finest place in the world in which to live. It provides a mechanism for leading thinkers and practitioners from many sectors of Canadian society to work together, to build consensus and help set the standards for a sustainable future. We improve this mechanism successfully dealing with the environmental and economic challenges that face us through this particular piece of legislation. I am very pleased that my colleague from Broadview- Greenwood is nodding his head in agreement to this initiative. We are very pleased for the support of the opposition.
Many developing nations are considering the Canadian round table as a model institution to assist them in designing and implementing policies for more environmentally sustainable forms of development. Several states within the United States are taking a careful look at copying our round table model as a means to address some of their most controversial and pressing environmental and economic challenges.
The round table model is the opportunity for participation and consensus building. Let me say that the greatest challenge of sustainable development is to apply more effectively the full range of human intelligence, knowledge and experience to the problems that we will face in the coming decades.
It is critical for us to increase the opportunity for Canadians to participate in the decisions that affect them all. We have had some outstanding members sitting around the Canadian round table for the last few years. Dr. George Connell, the former president of the University of Toronto is the present chairman of the round table.
This piece of legislation gives us the opportunity of putting this institution into legislative form. Sustainable development will require a democratization of decisionmaking beyond the comfortable status quo.
Compartmentalization of responsibility no longer works. We cannot put everything just in compartments. It is a holistic approach. Cross-sectoral, cross-disciplinary and cross-jurisdictional thinking is a better way to deal with an uncertain future and round tables reflect that reality.
This act will sanction the importance and continuing existence of the national round table. Bill C-72 will validate and encourage the continuing support of the private sector and others for this new form of public involvement.
Passage of Bill C-72 will enable this organization to retain the private sector support so essential to its success. Many sectors of Canadian society and business have made substantial personal commitments and organizational contribution to the work of the national round table.
Now this national round table must have greater autonomy to continue to build partnerships independent of government for the benefit of all Canadians. Providing that independence through Bill C-72 will allow the national round table to maintain its distinctive nature separate from government direction but with the full commitment of government as partner.
By empowering the members of the national round table, government can promote the understanding and trust that leads to a well-considered, honest and direct advice that is grounded in the real world.
The national round table is an important step in the continuing transition to sustainable development in Canada. As an institutional experiment it has a proven track record and has wide international support. Many of the most important groups affecting Canada's environment and economy are involved in support of the work of the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy.
With the consent of the House of Commons, Canadians will look back on this day with pride as the day our nation again took the lead on the long road to a sustainable future.

advisory councils and bodies, particularly those that might offer creative and accurate criticism of this government's policies and practices. The second reason is this government's track record on the environment.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to pursue a question which I have asked in the House on a number of occasions of the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning the tragic plight of two young Canadians, Christine Lamont and David Spencer.
I am sure that members of this House are well aware of the fact that Christine and David were victims of a harsh and quite unfair Brazilian justice system which resulted in sentences of 28 years of imprisonment for each of them.

March 11, 1993
Adjournment Debate
That would be bad enough but in addition, because of the lack of response of the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs, their injustice at the hands of the Brazilian system has been compounded by the injustice of their own Canadian government.
I am sure that Canadians from coast to coast to coast have rallied to speak out in support of Christine and David in their struggle and I really want to pay tribute to those Canadians and in particular to the families of Christine and David who have waged a tireless and energetic campaign on their behalf.
The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs has twice urged the Secretary of State for External Affairs to finally recognize the injustice of the situation and to seek the remedy of expulsion which is provided by the Brazilian constitution. The minister has refused to do so. She wrings her hands and says we are waiting for the transfer of offenders treaty to be ratified. Then she says she is waiting for the appeals to be dealt with and it will be done soon. Meanwhile, we are still waiting for that transfer of offenders treaty. The appeals which were supposed to be heard this week we are now told will be heard some time, maybe next week. The support for Christine and David grows. Meanwhile, the threats to their health and safety are even greater.
I was very pleased to note that recently, just in early January, representatives and leaders of four Canadian churches wrote to the Prime Minister urging that the Prime Minister do the right thing and seek expulsion. The original letter was written by Archbishop Edwin Lackey the day before his sudden death on behalf of Archbishop Marcel Gervais, the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Ottawa and the chair of the Catholic Conference of Bishops. It was signed by the Moderator of the United Church of Canada and the Moderator of the Presbyterian Church of Canada as well. They have not even had the courtesy of a reply.
This injustice demands a response from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Brazil has said it does not understand why the Canadian government has not made a request for expulsion. The former minister of justice, a very respected individual, Mr. Harbez Piccarino, recognized the injustices in the case and he has recommended expulsion.
The time that Christine and David have already spent in prison would qualify them for a parole if they were eligible for parole. As foreigners they are not eligible for parole, however. These sentences are cruel and unusual treatment. The original convictions were an appalling injustice.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, who apparently is thinking about seeking the leadership, of becoming Prime Minister of Canada, cannot even act on behalf of two young Canadians, Christine Lamont and David Spencer, who are entitled to justice. She does not even deserve to be Secretary of State for External Affairs, let alone the Prime Minister of Canada.
I want to again take this opportunity to appeal through you to the government to recognize the injustice of the situation of Christine and David, to heed the unanimous appeal of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and to at last, finally, seek the expulsion of Christine and David from Brazil so they can return home to their loved ones.
These young Canadians are respected individuals. They have no criminal record whatsoever and a terrible injustice has been done. I hope that this government will finally show the leadership it so far has been lacking.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Guilbault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the member for Burnaby-Kingsway, who sits with me on the external affairs committee, for his interest in the case of these two young Canadians outside the country who are detained through a miscarriage of justice.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs set out her views on this case in letters dated August 13 and December 8, 1992 to the chairman of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General.
It cannot be assumed that if Canada asked for the expulsion of Christine Lamont and David Spencer, it would be granted automatically. While the Brazilian President has the discretionary authority to grant expulsion, it has been emphasized to us that there is a clear distinction between the authority as set out in the Brazilian constitution and the practice according to which the authority is exercised.
March 11, 1993

We have been told that in principle, expulsion would not be granted while appeals are under way or before the convicted prisoner has served his or her sentence.
We have also been told that the Brazilian government would not agree to expulsion in these circumstances because it would amount to unwarranted interference by the executive branch of government in the affairs of the judiciary and would discriminate against the other defendants who would not be released or expelled.
On many occasion, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has expressed concern over the severity of the sentences received by Miss Lamont and Mr. Spencer. These sentences, and the convictions themselves, are being appealed in the Brazilian courts.
The Canadian embassy in Brasilia has been working actively to ensure that both the appeal of the convictions and the appeal of the sentences move forward as quickly as possible. The Brazilian courts are now in session. The embassy will continue to do all it can to ensure that the appeal process keeps moving expeditiously.
The embassy's efforts to hasten the ratification of the transfer of offenders treaty between Canada and Brazil which was signed last July 15 have also been achieving some success. The treaty would enable Miss Lamont and Mr. Spencer to serve the rest of their sentences in Canadian facilities, where they would be subject to Canadian parole laws. As you know the treaty was approved by the Foreign Relations Committee of the Chamber of Deputies in December and will be considered by the Justice Committee when it reconvenes under a new chairman this month.
The embassy has been assured of support for the treaty both in the justice committee and in the Senate which will consider it following approval in the justice committee.

Mr. Speaker, in questioning the Prime Minister on December 1, 1992 I wanted to address some of the concerns that have arisen in Nova Scotia and across Canada with respect to the
Adjournment Debate
tragedy in the Westray coal mine in Pictou County, Nova Scotia.
For the record let me express the sympathy shared by all Canadians for the widows, families, and friends of the 26 miners whose lives were ended by the mine explosion that occurred at 5.20 in the morning of May 9, 1992, another tragic day in the bitter history of coal mining in Nova Scotia. These brave men will not be forgotten but their memories will be preserved with those who perished at Springhill, in Cape Breton and elsewhere in mining disasters.
I hope what I will now say will not in any way add to the grief or detract from the hopes for the future of our mining families. Let me begin by stating my concern for and solidarity with these family members and friends who seek a just accounting for the Westray disaster. I am shocked and disturbed by the chain of events that left widows, parents and children asking whether there is any justice for them and the deceased miners.
Even recognizing the needs of people and even realizing that only employment opportunities will satisfy many of these needs, let me say clearly and categorically it is my view that Westray and its parent corporation, Cur-ragh Resources Inc., must be separated totally and completely from government funded mining operations in Pictou County. I can envision no hope whatever that this organization can resolve the problems associated with management of this coal resource and I can see nothing but grief from continuing the involvement of Westray and Curragh.
Let me be very specific. Not one more cent of taxpayers' money, federally or provincially, should be directed to Westray or Curragh. Certainly the $16 million apparently available from insurers should be held for the benefit of the people involved in the mine operation and not the corporate owners. In fact the appropriate government authorities should separate Westray and Curragh from the mine assets and seek recovery of the moneys lost from whatever assets the corporations may have left.
I ask simply: How can a corporate organization cause a taxpayers' loss in the area of $100 million and still claim dominion over a public resource?

March 11, 1993
Adjournment Debate
Let me state some other points related to the Westray mine disaster that must shock the grieving families and demand public attention.
First, Curragh sought to dispose of the Westray mine in November 1991 according to Maclean's magazine in order to improve its financial position, showing that the corporation had no real commitment to Nova Scotia or its people.
Second, there is mounting evidence that the coal resource cannot be mined economically without real risk to the lives and safety of miners or without further massive government aid that would be better utilized elsewhere.
Third, if there is a determination to mine the coal seam at Plymouth it is clear that the operation should be turned over to an organization with an established record for safety and fair employment practice.
Now let me address what has become the unfortunate politicization of the Westray tragedy. When the explosion occurred the premier of Nova Scotia immediately responded by saying there would be a full and complete public inquiry by way of a royal commission. This action by the premier has proved to be as destructive and demoralizing as the mining tragedy itself. Let me tell the House why.
First, the premier of Nova Scotia must have known that the provisions of the Coal Mines Regulation Act require an immediate investigation of a mine fatality and a report on the apparent cause. Had this statutory process proceeded there would have been a factual and public report that could have been examined and then amplified by subsequent further inquiry.
Second, it is inexcusable that the premier's advisers were not aware of the Supreme Court decision in the Patricia Starr case. This case received national attention and severely restricted public inquiries in circumstances that might produce criminal charges. From the very beginning there was an indication that criminal negligence was involved. The province should have known a broad based inquiry beyond the Coal Mines Regulation Act would be derailed by the courts.
What is left for the grieving families and the public? Over the months an RCMP investigation was announced and charges were laid under provincial safety laws and
later stayed. The over-all impression is one of legal incompetency on the part of ministers and officials. Criminal negligence is a simple charge under the Criminal Code involving only proof of legal duty to act carefully and evidence of wanton or reckless disregard for life in performing the duty.
Here are my recommendations: Get rid of Westray-Curragh, make the case for criminal negligence, find another mine operator. Let me add this. The royal commission, whatever its good intentions, will add nothing to solace the widows and families of the deceased miners and it will not benefit those who follow them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Guilbault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Halifax West for his question. I would like to commend him for his interest in this issue.
The federal government provided assistance to Westray principally in the form of loan insurance as well as an interest rate buy-down on that same loan. The assistance was provided because the development of the mine, with its potential to create approximately 240 new jobs, was a regional development priority for the government.
Our involvement was strictly financial in nature. The extent of the federal government's jurisdiction with respect to this project was limited and did not include mining regulations or occupational health and safety issues.
The regulation of mines, under the Constitution is a provincial responsibility and pertains to all aspects of mine plan approval and monitoring. The only exceptions are the Cape Breton Development Corporation and uranium mines.
The Government of Nova Scotia established a commission of inquiry with the mandate to examine events leading up to the accident and to establish the cause of the accident. In order to assist the commission the federal government undertook the enormous task of compiling and cataloguing all federal government documents related to the Westray project. This involved
24.000	pages of documents dating back several years.
Prior to the constitutional challenge of the commission
8.000	pages of closing documents had been released. Initially, the Nova Scotia Supreme Court ruled that the commission, under its original terms of reference, was unconstitutional.
March 11, 1993

The decision was appealed by both the miners' union and the Nova Scotia government. In the ruling by the appeals division of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court in January 1993 the status of the commission was confirmed as valid. Once the criminal investigation by the RCMP is complete and any subsequent charges are dealt with the commission will be free to resume hearings.
The federal government will fully co-operate with any agency mandated by the Government of Nova Scotia to find the causes of the accident at the Westray coal mine.

Mr. Speaker, in his financial statement of December 2 the Minister of Finance said the following: "Funding will be increased for the highly successful Industrial Research Assistance Program which provides technology support and financial assistance to businesses".
On February 25 I quoted that to the Minister of Finance and asked him why the estimates showed that the Industrial Research Assistance Program was cut by $1,333 million.
The answer to the question was provided by the Minister of State for Science who said that there had been an increase of $14 million for science and technology. That was a very interesting answer because it did not refer to the Industrial Research Assistance Program at all.
On February 26 I repeated that question quoting again from the December 2, 1992 statement and we got this peculiar answer from the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology.
I tell my hon. friend that we were both right yesterday. First, S and T funding has gone up considerably over last year. He still did not answer the question about IRAP, but I did point out that if there were in fact a $14 million increase in science and technology in the face of an over-all rate of government expenditures of approximately $5 billion, that really did not amount to very much.
Adjournment Debate
The minister of state came back to answer the question of what happened to the funds that were promised for IRAP and indicated that IRAP spending would be the same or up. "This is a very important program", he says. "I agree with the hon. member. We are defusing technology in an unprecedented way. It is a core part of what we are trying to do under S and T."
He says he is going to somehow backfill IRAP in order to bring it up, if it is going to go up. Moments ago after many calls to the minister's office we got what he was referring to, and what he was referring to was the National Research Council estimates which from the 1992-93 Main Estimates to the 1993-94 estimates indicate about a $14 million increase in grants and contributions.
However, that is not an answer to the question about expenditures in science and technology because if we look at science and technology generally there have been a number of cuts, not the least of which was the revocation of the 4 per cent increases given to the granting councils, in addition to the decrease in IRAP, the $13 million cut in the DIPP, the $4.75 million cut in NSERC-that is beyond the 4 per cent revocation of an increase-and the SSHRC budget was cut by $582,000. If he is talking about science and technology surely the answer he has provided to me today does not answer the question about science and technology.
I really would like somebody to answer the question: How is it the Minister of Finance promised an increase in IRAP but in fact IRAP was cut? I want to know why there is this inconsistency. I do not want another non sequitur as was provided by the Minister for Science. I do not want another non sequitur as was provided to those others in this adjournment debate who have been trying to get clarity in response to their questions.
If the parliamentary secretary is going to do the same to me as he did to them, he can spare his time because it will be a non-answer. We will still not understand why the minister made his promise and failed to meet it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Guilbault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Windsor-St. Clair for his question. I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on behalf of the government on this important program.

March 11, 1993
Adjournment Debate
There is no doubt the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program, IRAP, is an outstanding success that we should build upon. Few people in Canadian industry would question IRAP's significant benefits in terms of jobs, exports and new technologies. Although IRAP could clearly do more with increased funding, it is important to note that IRAP has done extremely well during a period of strict restraint in government spending. Not only has it been maintained but it has received increases in its funding. An allocation of the additional $27 million was announced last year.
Additional funding and strengthening of IRAP's role were also among the commitments made by the Minister of Finance in his December economic statement. Although this new funding is not included in the Main Estimates, decisions on the price levels will be made soon and will be announced in due course.
This will be a substantial recognition of our values and potential. Two years ago some concerns were expressed over the new strategic plan on the program. But evidence now shows that the plan was the right way to go.
Our most recent annual report shows a 5 per cent increase in the number of its projects. There is improvement in efficiency and a clear focus on IRAP's premier clientele for small and medium size businesses. IRAP is now in a good position to assume an even stronger role in building national competitiveness.
The government has already committed itself to ensuring that IRAP has the power and the resources it needs.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to follow up a question I asked of the Minister of National Defence on peacekeeping. I appreciate that in Question Period there is a very short time for questions and indeed for answers.
I felt it necessary to follow up on this because I have a legitimate concern and whether it trends out or not is to be seen as the history book unfolds. I am not claiming to be any visionary but I do see certain trends that bother
me. I am speaking out tonight because I am not sure there has been a total recognition of the two conflicting trends that bother me.
The first one is on the subject of peacekeeping and the very fact that in the last four years we have seen as many peacekeeping operations take place as we have in the last 40 years. That is an indicator in itself.
There is the very fact that at last count we have 179 countries in the world today. Of these countries, only 10 per cent of them have any homogeneity in their populations. Of that 10 per cent, only half have ethnic groups that account for 75 per cent of the population. In other words, most of these countries have very small, chopped up ethnic groups. We are seeing it in the world today. We are seeing what amounts to tribalism. It is not a question of countries fighting countries; it is a question of tribes fighting tribes. Sometimes they forget why they are fighting.
If you add to this an increasing problem with social intolerance, cultural and ethnic intolerance, I believe you are going to see the requirement for more and more peacekeeping operations throughout the world. Not only will it be more peacekeeping operations but different kinds of peacekeeping operations. We have already seen a deviation from the standard peacekeeping operation like that in Cyprus to now what is certainly the edge of peacemaking, humanitarian support, food control and that kind of thing.
The point I am making is that peacekeeping is increasing and the nature of peacekeeping is increasing.
Another point is that I believe, as this continues to increase, like-minded countries are going to have difficulties coping with this.
We now have roughly 4,500 troops participating in peacekeeping operations. Canada has participated in every single one of them and I think that is great. Our contribution to international peace is laudatory. Soon the time will come, and I believe we are very close to it, closer than we would care to admit, where we will not be able to participate. I believe that for the following reasons.
March 11, 1993

At the time we were preparing for the cold war. This is nobody's fault. You cannot plan for uncertainty and be right all the time. Three years ago we decided to close our bases in Europe. We decided to reduce the army by around 4,000 and we took other measures with respect to equipment.
As the facts show those decisions perhaps in retrospect were not the best ones. The fact remains we did take those decisions. Another decision was the total force concept where we used more reserves to make up the standing army and navy. A good decision. It was a good one and continues to be good.
Right now, because we are short of regular force troops, we have three major army groups deployed right now, 4,700 troops. We had only planned ever to have
2,000	when we had 4,000 more soldiers. That in itself is a very dangerous trend.
We are going to have to have a very close look at the increasing demands on our peacekeepers. We are going to have to have a look at the difficult areas we are getting into with respect to the number of regular force soldiers we have and what level at reserve and militia force should we supplement them.
There is also the equipment. I just came from a defence committee meeting where there was some concern shown by the expert witness on the kind of equipment we have, whether it was the right kind of equipment and whether or not it was deployed in the right manner.
In summary and conclusion of my remarks here this evening, I would like to ask purely and simply and in a non-partisan manner that the Minister of National Defence be cognizant of the increasing trend and the demand on Canadians because of our expertise and record in peacekeeping. She should look at the trend on decisions that were taken which would permit us to less and less be able to contribute to more and more. She should take cognizance of that and respond with perhaps a new defence statement or new priorities of defence that will show how we are going to cope with that. Before we commit any other sizeable groups of Canadian soldiers, sailors or airmen I believe that there has to be a full discussion in Parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Guilbault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception for raising this important matter and I welcome this opportunity to respond on behalf of the Minister of National Defence.
Adjournment Debate
The priorities identified in our defence policy published in April 1992 are based on our commitments to the defence of Canada, domestic security, arms control and disarmament, and peaceful dispute settlement.
In a field in which Canada has been active for the past 40 years, our peacekeepers have acquired a reputation for professionalism that is recognized the world over. Our contribution to UN peacekeeping operations is a source of great pride to the members of our armed forces.
It is an indication of the trust we enjoy on the international scene and of the support in this country for our efforts to maintain world peace. It is true that certain specialties are in great demand. Nevertheless, our regular and reserve forces are capable of meeting our various commitments. As for the ability of our reservists to perform their duties in the armed forces as a whole, so far we have had no trouble finding the necessary numbers to bring our regular forces up to the strength required to perform these missions effectively.
At the present time, the system works. Peacekeeping operations are reviewed regularly which means that resources assigned to the various missions are reviewed and modified as appropriate.

At the moment there are some 4,700 Canadians taking part in peacekeeping operations around the world. Of these, approximately 475 are members of the reserve. Under total force, increasing numbers of reservists will be available to take part in peacekeeping operations. These troops are well-trained, prepared members of the Canadian forces and ready to serve alongside their regular force counterparts under any circumstances.
As evidence of our commitment to making total force work, in 1993-94 total expenditures of the primary reserve will rise by nearly $46 million over the forecast in the current financial year. This is a 6 per cent increase. In addition capital expenditures of the primary reserve will rise to 25.6 per cent of the total reserve expenditures, up from 16.1 per cent in the last fiscal year's estimates.
The purchase of new equipment will ensure that the Canadian forces, reserve and regular alike, will have what they need to fulfil their roles, both at home and abroad. Important acquisitions include many types of equipment which will be used to ensure the safety of our troops on peacekeeping operations.

I will repeat what the Minister of National Defence said not long ago when she appeared before the Standing

March 11, 1993
Adjournment Debate
Committee on National Defence, namely that the government is considering some new approaches to participation in peacekeeping missions throughout the world.
Again, I wish to thank the hon. member for raising this question which is of interest to us all. I trust I was able to provide the requisite clarification.
